kaigo-atomic-standing-cane.heading: Support for standing and cane-walking sequences
paragraphs: Before standing, check physical condition and possible movements, explain the assistance and obtain consent. In the material’s hemiplegia example, the person sits a little nearer the seat edge, draws the unaffected foot back and leans the upper body forward to begin standing. The idea is to move the center of gravity into a supported area and make it easier to bear weight on the unaffected side.

In this example the care worker stands on the affected side and provides support to prevent knee buckling and falls. Knee buckling means that the knee bends because it cannot support the body during standing or walking. After substantial changes in body or head position, check dizziness, how the person feels and changes in physical condition.

The three-step cane-walking example separates “cane, affected foot, unaffected foot.” Two-step walking groups “cane and affected foot, then unaffected foot.” The material presents three-step walking as a more stable example, but do not change the number of steps for speed alone without assessing the person’s strength, equipment and actual walking.

In the hemiplegic walking-assistance example, the care worker stays behind the affected side and supports the upper body or waist as needed. Connect starting with the affected foot to its reason: the unaffected side supports the body at the start. Specific support methods and the amount of help must follow the individual plan and practical training.

The ascending-step example follows “cane, unaffected foot, affected foot”; descending follows “cane, affected foot, unaffected foot.” The care worker is shown on a lower step than the person, behind when ascending and in front when descending. The position one step below describes that illustration’s conditions. Confirm the method according to handrails, step, cane and the person’s abilities.

Remembering only “unaffected foot first when going up” does not explain cane or helper positions. This text teaches how to read sequences and reasons; it is not a manual for trying unfamiliar assistance. Do not force the illustrated form on someone whose weight-bearing or joint conditions do not suit it. If they feel unwell or cannot be supported adequately, do not persist; request help or professional confirmation.

kaigo-atomic-wheelchair-transfer.heading: Separate transfer preparation, performance and wheelchair travel
paragraphs: Transferring from bed to wheelchair differs from pushing the wheelchair after the person is seated. Check condition, required staffing, what the person can do, equipment and method, then explain and obtain consent. Do not record completed wheelchair preparation as a completed transfer.

The material’s hemiplegia example places the wheelchair on the unaffected side and applies the brakes while it is stationary. Check in advance the support used by the unaffected hand and the assistance preventing buckling of the affected knee. Check wheelchair and floor condition too; positioning alone does not establish safety.

The material shows using the unaffected hand to hold the far arm support, moving the upper body forward while standing, turning toward the wheelchair and sitting. Standing, turning and sitting each require support suited to individual abilities and methods. This is not an instruction to independently stand or turn someone unable to bear weight.

In the material’s example, after the person sits well back and their feet are supported on foot supports, the worker checks how they feel and their condition. In practice, check seating depth, body support, foot position and the state of hands and clothing according to the person and wheelchair. Do not conclude assistance is complete merely because they are seated; connect observations of sustainable comfort and sliding with the plan.

Before pushing, check whether the feet can rest on the foot supports and whether hands or clothing might catch in the wheels. The example places the unaffected hand on the arm support and the affected hand inside it. Check this example against the posture the person can maintain and the equipment’s conditions.

Before starting, tell the person the wheelchair will move and release the brakes according to the confirmed procedure. When stopping, check the brakes, surroundings and the person’s condition too. Actual transfers and travel follow the individual plan, wheelchair instructions and training. Never record a stage not yet performed as completed.

kaigo-atomic-wheelchair-curb.heading: Read direction and sequence in curb and slope illustrations
paragraphs: Stop before a curb or step and explain what will happen. In the ascending example, the material shows placing a foot on the tipping lever and moving the push handles diagonally downward to raise the front. Read the sequence as placing the front wheels slowly onto the step before raising the rear wheels.

The descending example travels backward. It shows slowly lowering the rear wheels first, then lowering the front wheels under control after the rear wheels have cleared the step. For descent too, the illustration shows a foot pressing the tipping lever while the push handles are pulled diagonally downward to control tilt. The front–rear sequence differs from ascent. This explains how to read the source illustration. Actual handling requires checks of equipment, route and individual conditions and must follow the trained method.

For a steep downward slope, the example shows moving backward to help prevent the person sliding forward off the seat. The care worker checks safety behind and takes a supporting stance with the feet apart front to back. Check whether the route can actually be used and how, considering wheelchair type, slope, helpers’ strength and staffing.

Distinguish the force direction shown by arrows, the wheelchair’s travel direction and the front–rear wheel sequence. Raising the front wheels differs from deciding when to set them down. The example also controls lowering slowly; it does not mean that more force makes every step passable.

This teaches illustration reading under the material’s conditions, not self-taught practice with a person in the wheelchair. Do not use foot supports as steps or force passage over unsuitable curbs or slopes. Follow the plan and practical training for the route, equipment and support method; ask the person responsible if anything is unclear.

kaigo-atomic-swallow-stages.heading: Five stages of eating and swallowing
paragraphs: Meals provide energy and nutrients that support life and bodily activity. They also offer enjoyment of flavors, daily rhythm and connection with others. Food being in front of someone does not establish that the needed nutrients have entered their body.

In the anticipatory stage before eating, the person recognizes food by seeing color and shape or smelling its aroma, and saliva secretion prepares for eating. The brain contributes to hunger and the desire to eat. This is not a stage in which food has already reached the stomach.

In the preparatory stage, food in the mouth is chewed and mixed with saliva to form a bolus: food gathered together for swallowing. In the following oral stage, mainly the tongue moves the bolus toward the throat. Distinguish chewing from sending food out of the mouth.

In the pharyngeal stage, the swallowing reflex occurs and the bolus passes through the pharynx. Rather than viewing the epiglottis as a separate lid acting alone, understand this as a stage in which the larynx and related muscles coordinate to protect the airway while food moves toward the esophagus.

In the esophageal stage, the bolus travels through the esophagus to the stomach. A difficulty in any anticipatory, preparatory, oral, pharyngeal or esophageal stage may affect safe eating. Observing chewing or throat movement alone does not establish that all stages and airway safety have been checked.

A meal connects moving to the eating place, maintaining posture, recognizing food, holding utensils, bringing food to the mouth, chewing and swallowing. Do not take over every part because one is difficult. Distinguish what the person can do from the help needed.

Appearance and aroma contribute to food recognition, taste to flavor, and touch to mouthfeel and texture. Recognizing or liking food differs from confirming swallowing function. Support follows individual assessment and the plan; tell professionals what you observed if changes occur.

kaigo-atomic-food-devices.heading: Distinguish the purposes of textures, posture and eating aids
paragraphs: Chopping, pureeing and softening while retaining shape are different adjustments. Distinguish unthickened liquids from thickened ones too. Match them to assessed chewing and swallowing abilities and the individual plan. Labels such as fine, soft or liquid alone do not establish safety.

The material’s chair example shows sitting well back with the soles supported, leaning slightly forward and positioning the chin down. A raised-chin example illustrates risk and prompts a review of helper position too. Do not force one identical form on everyone; follow the assessed upper-body, head and chin position for the individual.

For eating in bed, confirm the individual method for supporting the upper body and head. The material shows supporting and settling the body back onto the bedding after raising the back section. Study this in relation to reducing sliding and pressure. Actual movement must follow a trained method suited to the person. The side-lying example places the unaffected side underneath and supports the head with a pillow, but a diagnosis alone does not determine lying direction or posture.

Posture illustrations are examples for understanding support. Do not independently pull or lift the person to reproduce a pictured shape; follow equipment instructions, the assessed method and practical training. Maintaining a posture alone does not prove safe swallowing.

Spoons and forks with easy-grip handles or retaining straps assist holding. Bent spoons and forks are shaped to make bringing food toward the mouth easier. Spring-assisted chopsticks support pinching movements. Observe how the person holds utensils and which part is difficult, then use the selected aid.

Easy-scoop plates help gather and lift food, while non-slip mats stabilize items on the table. Easy-hold bowls and cups with handles help with holding containers. Eating aids have different purposes; check which parts the person can do independently.

Being able to hold a cup tells you about hand movement; it does not establish that the drink’s consistency matches the swallowing plan. Check equipment suitability, food suitability and posture separately.

Consider the enjoyment of warm and cold foods, but still check the temperature at which the person will touch or eat them. Do not prioritize keeping food hot alone. Confirm temperature and texture suited to the person’s sensations and plan, and do not independently add water or thickener.

kaigo-atomic-meal-checks.heading: Checks before meals, between mouthfuls and afterward
paragraphs: Before a meal, check physical condition, explain the support and obtain consent. Verify that the meal is for this person and matches confirmed information on texture, treatment restrictions and allergies. Clean hands and place the tray where the person can recognize it. The illustrated helper position is diagonally in front on the dominant-hand or unaffected side.

Moistening the mouth before eating may be included in the plan. Although the material gives tea and soup as examples, this does not instruct staff to give thin liquids to everyone. The drink’s consistency and method must follow assessment and the plan. Workers must not give drinks to test swallowing function.

Match both mouthful size and the interval before the next mouthful to the person. Do not aim only to shorten the meal; observe posture, pace, utensil use, chewing, swallowing and wishes. Do not add another mouthful while the person is still dealing with the previous one.

The helper sits at a height and position that allows observation of the face and mouth without making the person look upward. In a hemiplegia example, the material shows assistance from the unaffected mouth corner and withdrawing the spoon horizontally. Understand why pulling food upward could make the person extend their neck; actual handling follows the individual method and training.

Ask about the menu and preferences at a suitable time when the person can speak. To help prevent aspiration, refrain from talking to them while they are chewing and wait until they can speak. Respect wishes to rest or finish; food remaining is not a reason to force continued eating.

Confirm with the person that the meal is finished, check for food remaining in the mouth and arrange suitable oral care. An empty plate alone does not establish who ate how much, whether the mouth is empty or whether nutrition was sufficient.

The material gives sitting for about 30 minutes after a meal as one example of a precaution against aspiration pneumonia. The actual resting position and duration follow the person’s condition and plan. A uniform number cannot replace assessment. Do not treat lying down immediately as the automatic next step; support the person using the confirmed method.

Clock positioning for someone with reduced vision uses directions from the person’s viewpoint. The far side is 12 o’clock, the near side 6, the right 3 and the left 9, with other numbers showing directions between them. Clock numbers describe position, not meal time or food amount.

Explain food names and locations as well as temperature and seasoning. Check whether the person finds this method understandable, and tell them again if food is moved. If the eating method does not suit their condition or they feel unwell, do not force continued support. Request help or professional assessment according to facility procedures.

kaigo-atomic-skin-structure.heading: Skin layers, sweat glands and care of skin folds
paragraphs: In a skin cross-section, distinguish the outer epidermis, dermis below it and deeper subcutaneous fatty tissue. Hair roots, sebaceous glands and sweat glands are not all arranged on the surface. Do not confuse the labeled structures with sweat or dirt on the skin surface itself.

Hair grows from the part within the follicle, and sebaceous glands secrete sebum. From the coiled sweat-gland part shown in cross-section, a duct runs to the surface and releases sweat. Distinguish the gland, duct and released sweat when reading the structure; the diagram does not diagnose gland condition from external appearance. Sebum and sweat help maintain the skin surface, but this does not mean secretions may remain indefinitely.

Eccrine sweat glands are widely distributed and help release heat through sweat. Apocrine glands occur in areas such as the armpits. Odor depends on more than gland names; breakdown of secretions by skin bacteria also contributes.

Skin cushions external impacts, protects internal organs and protects the body from irritation by harmful substances. It also senses stimuli and helps regulate temperature. Strong rubbing to remove dirt may damage the skin that needs protection. Consider both cleanliness and preservation of the skin.

Moisture and dirt can remain in creases and skin folds. Clean these gently according to their condition and remove moisture without rubbing. Sweat’s cooling function does not mean folded areas may be left damp for long periods.

The number of washes alone does not establish the result of care. Check cleanliness, dryness, redness, skin damage and the person’s pain or discomfort. Report changes specifically, and match methods to the person’s condition and support plan.

objectives: Explain the sequences and reasons for support in standing, cane-walking and step examples.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-standing-cane.prompt: Does “unaffected foot first when going up” fully explain the material’s cane-walking example?
options: Mentioning the unaffected foot explains cane-placement order too.
No. Cane placement, helper position and individual and equipment conditions are also needed.
The phrase also states whether the helper stands in front or behind.
Knowing the foot order means individual ability and step conditions are checked.
rationales: Foot order does not say when the cane is placed.
Foot order alone omits cane, helper and environment information, so it cannot determine the whole method.
The phrase contains no helper position; do not invent it from foot information.
Remembering a source sequence differs from checking that it suits the person and actual step.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-wheelchair-tran.prompt: After applying the brakes and positioning the wheelchair only, you recorded “transfer complete.” What should be corrected?
options: Adding the brake fact leaves “transfer complete” unchanged.
Record positioning as confirmation of the transfer direction and seated posture.
Because brakes were checked, the completed-transfer record includes how the person felt afterward.
Record preparation as complete, and separately record only confirmed transfer performance and seated condition.
rationales: More detailed preparation does not establish the unconfirmed result that the person actually transferred.
This extends equipment positioning to transfer and seated-posture checks not performed.
Brakes and how the person feels after transferring are separate checks; preparation does not establish their later feelings.
Preparation, the person’s transfer and subsequent condition and posture are different stages. Do not mark an unperformed result complete.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-wheelchair-curb.prompt: Why can’t “front wheels first” mean the same wheel order for both ascending and descending a step?
options: Both use the tipping lever, so only the helper’s position differs.
Diagonal downward handle arrows prevent comparison of wheel contact order.
Forward ascent and backward descent have different orders for placing or lowering the wheels.
“Backward” in the descent illustration refers only to the helper’s feet, not wheelchair travel.
rationales: Using the same part does not explain differences in travel direction or wheel contact order.
Force direction and wheel order are separate information; each wheel’s movement can be read.
The ascent example places front wheels first; backward descent lowers rear wheels first. Read travel direction with contact sequence.
The material shows the wheelchair descending backward, not only the direction of the helper’s feet.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-swallow-stages.prompt: Does chewing food alone confirm that it was swallowed safely?
options: No. Oral, pharyngeal and esophageal stages follow preparation, and airway protection needs separate checking.
Yes. Chewing shows that the pharyngeal stage ended normally too.
Yes. Forming a bolus and protecting the airway are the same check.
Yes. Observed chewing includes the result of food reaching the stomach through the esophagus.
rationales: Chewing is information about one stage, not every later passage or airway condition.
Chewing concerns preparation and does not establish pharyngeal passage or airway protection.
Bolus formation and airway protection during pharyngeal passage are related but different functions.
Chewing alone does not establish that subsequent esophageal passage was checked.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-food-devices.prompt: Do a non-slip mat and a bent spoon support the same difficulty?
options: Yes. Both only help with scooping and the direction toward the mouth.
No, but grip strength alone is enough to select between them.
No, but choosing a utensil name completes checks of eating ease.
No. A mat stabilizes table items; a bent spoon helps the direction toward the mouth. Choose according to the person’s movements.
rationales: A mat stabilizes items, rather than supporting the same movement direction as a bent spoon.
Slipping plates and the arm’s range toward the mouth matter too; grip alone cannot distinguish the purposes.
Choosing an aid differs from checking actual comfort and what the person can do with it.
This distinguishes the movement supported rather than names alone and uses retained abilities.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-meal-checks.prompt: Does an empty plate alone establish sufficient eating and no food left in the mouth?
options: It completes intake checks, leaving only a mouth check.
No. Check established intake separately from mouth residue and the person’s condition.
An empty plate observation includes the course and amount of the person’s eating.
An empty plate confirms the person wishes to finish.
rationales: Why it became empty and who ate how much require separate checking; amount is not established.
An empty plate is one observation, not proof of the whole eating process, mouth condition or adequate nutrition.
The plate’s current state differs from earlier intake history. Do not invent an unobserved process.
Ask to confirm the wish to finish; plate condition alone cannot establish the person’s words or intention.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-skin-structure.prompt: Should skin folds be rubbed strongly every time to keep them clean?
options: No. Clean gently according to skin condition, remove moisture and check redness and pain.
Equal wiping counts mean equal skin effects regardless of force.
Removing visible dirt establishes absence of redness and pain too.
Because sweat releases heat, moisture in folds does not need checking separately from cleanliness.
rationales: Cleanliness with damaged skin is not an appropriate result; check cleanliness and skin preservation together.
Count alone does not show friction force or personal skin condition, so equal burden cannot be assumed.
Dirt removal, undamaged skin and absence of pain each need separate checks.
Cooling does not eliminate effects of retained moisture in skin folds. Check both cleanliness and dryness.
